extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students, and researchers interested in American literary history and humor
extracted.subtask_description: An encyclopedic overview of the Algonquin Round Table: its origin as a practical joke, membership and activities (luncheons, games, pranks), notable collaborative works, criticisms, and cultural legacy. Useful for understanding the practices and public reception of an early-20th-century American humor circle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wisecracks, wordplay, and witticisms
rubrics_metrics.description: At these luncheons they engaged in wisecracks, wordplay, and witticisms that through the newspaper columns of Round Table members, were disseminated across the country.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This phrasing identifies the core stylistic elements of the group's humor (brief, clever verbal play). The passage links that style to public reach via members' newspaper columns, implying that memorable, quotable lines were a central output.

rubrics_metrics.name: Daily luncheon association / frequency of meeting
rubrics_metrics.description: Members ... met for lunch each day at the Algonquin Hotel from 1919 until roughly 1929.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article treats regular, daily association as a key structural feature that fostered creative exchange and collaboration; frequency and consistency of meetings are presented as enabling factors for sustained production of witticisms and joint projects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Origins in practical joke
rubrics_metrics.description: The group that would become the Round Table began meeting in June 1919 as the result of a practical joke carried out by theatrical press agent John Peter Toohey.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The origin story foregrounds prankishness and irreverence as formative cultural values; producing humor that begins from an irreverent or teasing stance is presented as characteristic of the group's identity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical jokes and elaborate pranks as activity
rubrics_metrics.description: A number of Round Tablers were inveterate practical jokers, constantly pulling pranks on one another...They had several copies made [of a portrait], each slightly more askew than the last, and would periodically secretly swap them out...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page presents ongoing, increasingly elaborate pranks as both pastime and creative practice; examples serve as models of social, performative humor that reinforced group bonds and public anecdotes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Games and parlor-game generated witticisms
rubrics_metrics.description: The group was devoted to games, including cribbage and poker...They also played charades...and the 'I can give you a sentence' game, which spawned Dorothy Parker's memorable sentence using the word horticulture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Games are described as generative devices for one-liners and quips; this suggests a criterion that playful, constrained prompts (parlor games) can create sharp, repeatable humor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collaborative theatrical production (revue) as measure of success
rubrics_metrics.description: The entire group worked together successfully only once, however, to create a revue called No Sirree!, which helped launch a Hollywood career for Round Tabler Robert Benchley.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Staging a revue or other collaborative theatrical project is presented as a tangible output and success metric; the article uses the revue's outcomes (e.g., Benchley's career) to demonstrate practical, career-making impact of group work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Media dissemination via members' newspaper columns
rubrics_metrics.description: …through the newspaper columns of Round Table members, were disseminated across the country.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text emphasizes the role of print media in amplifying the group's humor; having regular columns or other media platforms is treated as a mechanism for reaching a national audience and building reputation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criticism: logrolling and rehearsed witticisms
rubrics_metrics.description: Their critics accused them of logrolling, or exchanging favorable plugs of one another's works, and of rehearsing their witticisms in advance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article records contemporary criticisms that count against authenticity—exchanging favors and pre-rehearsed gags were seen as undermining spontaneous wit. This functions as an evaluative negative criterion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critique: 'just a lot of people telling jokes' vs. substantive literary achievement
rubrics_metrics.description: Dorothy Parker ... criticized the group: 'The Round Table was just a lot of people telling jokes and telling each other how good they were...There was no truth in anything they said. It was the terrible day of the wisecrack...'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The passage frames a judgment about depth and seriousness: being merely witty is contrasted with producing lasting literary work. The article then balances that critique by listing Pulitzer-winning members, implying a dual metric of 'wit' versus 'lasting literary contribution.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Measured legacy: awards, careers, and institutional recognition
rubrics_metrics.description: Round Table members and associates contributed to the literary landscape, including Pulitzer Prize–winning work...the films of Harpo and Benchley remain popular, and Parker is renowned for her short stories...The Algonquin Hotel ... was designated a New York City Historic Landmark...and a national literary landmark by the Friends of Libraries USA.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tangible indicators of legacy—major awards, enduring films/works, influential publications (The New Yorker), and official landmark designations—are presented as objective measures of the group's cultural impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Membership fluidity and social inclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: Membership was not official or fixed. Many others moved in and out of the Circle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article implies that membership criteria were informal and social rather than formal credentials; being part of the scene, collaborating, or associating socially were the practical inclusion standards.
